lead: >-
  The Petrohué River in Chile's Lake District flows out of Todos los Santos Lake toward the Reloncaví Estuary. ## Petrohué River: from a mountain lake to Reloncaví

The Petrohué River flows through Chile's Los Lagos Region. It begins at the western end of Todos los Santos Lake and reaches the Reloncaví Estuary near the village of Ralún. According to hydrographic information from Chile's Library of the National Congress, the river is about **36 km** long. Over this relatively short distance, narrow rapids give way to wooded banks and a broader river valley.

Tourism descriptions often reduce Petrohué to its famous cascades. Yet the [Petrohué Waterfalls](/chile/place/petrohue-waterfalls/) are **just one part of a longer river**. The distinction matters when choosing an excursion: a short waterfall walk, riverside sightseeing and water sports have different durations and requirements.

## Where Petrohué begins and why its sections differ

The river carries water from Todos los Santos Lake through an Andean valley toward Reloncaví. Near its source, amid mountains, it is part of the scenery of [Vicente Pérez Rosales National Park](/chile/place/vicente-perez-rosales-national-park/). Farther on, the channel passes forested slopes, tributaries and more open terrain.

| Section | Character |
|---|---|
| Source by the lake | Lake water and mountains |
| Cascades | Narrow rocky channel |
| Middle reaches | Riverbanks and tributaries |
| Lower reaches | Broader valley |

This describes the river's natural zones, not a walking route covering all 36 kilometers. Access varies from bank to bank, and in some places roads and visitor facilities are well away from the water.

Petrohué is often described as turquoise. Its color depends on light, water clarity and rainfall, so on a cloudy day the scenery may look different from the photographs. The river and its setting are reason enough to visit.

## How the river differs from Petrohué Waterfalls

At the cascades, water rushes noisily between dark volcanic rocks. This stretch is most often associated with a short visit on designated paths. Beyond the cascades lie other river landscapes. You may observe the channel from its banks, but activities on the water require checks of the location, water level and professional operating conditions.

A nature-focused day in [Chile's Lake District](/chile/) combines several landscapes. Wooded areas and [Osorno Volcano](/chile/place/osorno-volcano/) are close to the river. However, proximity on a map does not mean the same walking route reaches them or that they are included in an excursion's price.

## Riverside walks, rafting and fishing: three different experiences

**A walk beside the river** suits travelers who want to see the current, forests and volcanic rocks without a sporting challenge. Existing paths and authorized viewpoints are sufficient. On our [33-day Ada Tours journey through Peru, Bolivia and Chile](/multi-country/tour/south-america-luxury-33-days/), Petrohué is part of a nature day from Puerto Varas visiting the waterfalls and Osorno; we do not advertise separate rafting or fishing on this itinerary.

**Rafting** involves selecting a suitable section, checking water levels, and arranging guides and equipment. A river with cascades and strong currents is unsuitable for an unassessed independent outing. The availability of commercial water activities in the region must be checked separately from the accessibility of sightseeing paths.

**Sport fishing** is known on the lower reaches of Petrohué. Such a trip requires information on current licenses, permitted seasons and regulations for the particular waters. A standard sightseeing tour does not automatically include fishing services.

For a nature walk, explore the [Petrohué Waterfalls](/chile/place/petrohue-waterfalls/). To compare itineraries that include Lake District attractions, see the [Chile tours catalog](/chile/tour/).

## Practicalities for a trip from Puerto Varas

[Puerto Varas](/chile/place/puerto-varas/) is normally used as a base to explore the upper river. The road leads toward Ensenada and Petrohué. Where you stop depends on your objective: viewing the water safely, following an authorized walking trail or meeting the operator of a specialized activity.

Check access before traveling. **As of the review on October 18, 2026, CONAF reported that the Petrohué Waterfalls sector had been closed for maintenance since September 30, 2026, until further notice.** This does not mean the entire river is closed, but neither does it make the viewing paths at the cascades accessible. Check current rules for the specific bank and road you plan to use.

The water is cold, the current strong and rocks at the river's edge can be slippery. Even on an easy walk, approaching the water outside marked trails is dangerous. Bring a waterproof jacket and shoes with reliable grip; arrange rafting, fishing and other specialist activities separately.

## Frequently asked questions about the Petrohué River

### Where does Petrohué begin and end?

It flows out of Todos los Santos Lake and enters the Reloncaví Estuary near Ralún. Its length is approximately 36 km.

### Are the Petrohué River and Petrohué Waterfalls the same place?

The waterfalls are on the river but occupy only one stretch. Visitors usually choose the cascades for a short sightseeing stop; other activities require a suitable river section and confirmation of access conditions.

### Can I walk the entire length of the river?

Not on a conventional sightseeing walk. Petrohué passes through sections of the valley with varying bank access. Choose an existing route with a specific starting and finishing point.

### Is fishing included in a nature trip from Puerto Varas?

Only if it is explicitly listed in the itinerary. Our [Ada Tours journey](/multi-country/tour/south-america-luxury-33-days/) specifies a nature stop at Petrohué; a separate fishing program is not confirmed.

## Petrohué Waterfalls: where they are and what makes them special

[Petrohué Waterfalls](/chile/place/petrohue-waterfalls/) are cascades on the Petrohué River in the Los Lagos Region of southern Chile. Flowing through dense green forests, the water surges through narrow passages in dark volcanic rock. On a clear day, snow-capped [Osorno Volcano](/chile/place/osorno-volcano/) appears on the horizon. The combination of rock, current and forested banks gives the cascades their recognizable appearance.

The word "waterfalls" may suggest a single sheer wall of falling water. Petrohué is different: **several turbulent flows and drops** move through a rocky channel. The best way to appreciate their shapes is from the established viewpoints, rather than trying to find a route down to the water.

## Why does the water run between black rocks?

The Petrohué River begins at Todos los Santos Lake. At the cascades, the current meets resistant volcanic rock and passes through narrow channels. The contrast between dark stone, foaming water and green forest is particularly vivid after rainfall and as the light changes.

Turquoise should not be expected at every hour: clouds, precipitation and changing water conditions affect the color. For travelers, seeing the powerful current against an Andean volcanic landscape matters more than the promise of a particular shade.

The cascades form part of the [Petrohué River](/chile/place/petrohue-river/) system, but **visiting the waterfalls is not the same as rafting the river**. A tour on the viewing paths and a separate activity on the water require different arrangements, equipment and access.

## Getting there from Puerto Varas and what to combine with the visit

Trips often begin in [Puerto Varas](/chile/place/puerto-varas/). The road runs east toward Ensenada and Petrohué along CH-225. In this part of [Vicente Pérez Rosales National Park](/chile/place/vicente-perez-rosales-national-park/), a day trip can include several distinct sights.

| Stop | Main experience |
|---|---|
| Waterfalls | Fast-moving cascades and rock |
| [Osorno](/chile/place/osorno-volcano/) | Volcano and mountain panoramas |
| Todos los Santos Lake | Water among the mountains |
| [Puerto Varas](/chile/place/puerto-varas/) | Llanquihue Lake and the town |

One active Ada Tours itinerary includes the waterfall area together with the park and Osorno on a dedicated day. See our [long journey through Peru, Bolivia and Chile](/multi-country/tour/south-america-luxury-33-days/) for an example of how this attraction fits into a longer tour. For other trip durations, use the [Chile tours catalog](/chile/tour/).

## Access to the falls: a current check is essential

**As of October 18, 2026, CONAF reported that the Saltos del Petrohué sector had been closed since September 30, 2026, for infrastructure maintenance until further notice.** This notice concerns that particular sector; decisions affecting other parts of the park must be checked separately. Before traveling, confirm reopening, tickets and visiting hours on the official CONAF and Pases Parques pages.

Do not assume the viewing platforms will be accessible simply because a stop is listed in a tour description. We can coordinate a nature day around places that are actually open, with any route changes and travel terms agreed before departure.

Even after reopening, wet surfaces, crowds and restrictions on some paths need to be considered. Do not leave authorized routes beside the rushing water for photographs.

## When to see the cascades

The Lake District has wet weather throughout the year. Choose your conditions based on whether there is enough time for the journey and whether open paths are safe for pedestrians. The cascades can look impressive under cloud, while Osorno's panorama is clearer in sunny weather. These experiences can be enjoyed on separate stops rather than trying to fit everything into one photograph.

Bring a waterproof jacket, shoes with non-slip soles and protection for your camera or phone against spray. Walking requires different preparation from rafting on the [Petrohué River](/chile/place/petrohue-river/); a sightseeing walk in the itinerary does not imply that water sports are included.

## Frequently asked questions about Petrohué Waterfalls

### Are the waterfalls inside a national park?

Yes. The cascades lie within [Vicente Pérez Rosales National Park](/chile/place/vicente-perez-rosales-national-park/) on the Petrohué River. Access is governed by protected-area rules and the status of the particular sector.

### Can I currently reach the viewpoints?

Check before traveling. On October 18, 2026, CONAF reported a closure of the sector dating from September 30, 2026, until further notice. Reopening other areas of the national park does not in itself confirm access to the cascades.

### Does a trip to the waterfalls include rafting?

No. The name alone does not imply this. An itinerary may include only a regular walk to the lookouts. Rafting is a separate activity whose availability and conditions must be agreed explicitly.

## Pia Glacier: a wall of ice among Tierra del Fuego's mountains

**Pia Glacier is known for its great mass of ice descending from the Darwin Mountains to the waters of the fjord bearing its name.** It lies in Chilean Tierra del Fuego, near the northwestern arm of the Beagle Channel. Visitors approach by sea: the ship enters the fjord, then passengers transfer to small inflatable boats for a landing if conditions permit.

Unlike a glacier that can be reached by road and viewed from a distant lookout, Pia is a destination on **an expedition through channels and fjords**. The passage by water is a substantial part of the experience: rocky shores narrow the view, and the glacier appears against mountain slopes.

On our [Fjords of Tierra del Fuego itinerary](/multi-country/tour/tierra-del-fuego-fjords/), Pia is visited on day three, after [Ainsworth Bay](/chile/place/ainsworth-bay/) and [Tucker Islets](/chile/place/tucker-islets/). After the fjord, the journey continues along Glacier Alley, allowing travelers to compare one glacier close up with a series of ice masses seen from the deck on the same day.

## What visitors can see at the glacier

### Ice front, rocks and fjord

Blue hues are particularly visible in crevasses and denser parts of the ice, while snow and surface ice appear lighter. Water, dark rock and snowy mountains create a sharp contrast. Small ice floes near the shore shift with currents and wind, so the fjord never looks exactly the same twice.

Tierra del Fuego's glaciers are connected with the snow and ice fields of the Darwin mountain range. They move slowly under their own weight, carry rock debris and form moraines. Observing such a valley reveals a geological process barely visible in everyday urban scenery.

However, **approaching the ice front at an arbitrary distance is dangerous**. Large blocks may break away, and waves and currents require a safe distance. The crew decides the boat route and authorized landing places.

### Viewpoint and moraine

Our itinerary offers shore options with different physical demands. The shorter walk leads to a glacier lookout. Another route climbs a lateral moraine over uneven, rocky ground.

The short option suits travelers who chiefly want to see the glacier and fjord from above. The moraine climb appeals more to active walkers, but requires confidence moving over rocks and an assessment of trail conditions. Even the easier walk is not a paved path: landing takes place from a boat onto a natural shore.

If you find steps or uneven ground difficult, check participation requirements separately. **Independent glacier walks, ice climbing and walking on the glacier's surface are not advertised in this itinerary.**

## Pia Glacier versus Glacier Alley: what is the difference?

Pia is a specific destination where a landing and walk may be included. **Glacier Alley** is a section of the sea passage along the Beagle Channel with views of several glaciers on its northern side. These names therefore refer to different ways of experiencing the ice.

At Pia, travelers may leave the deck for a land-based viewpoint and observe the glacial valley. On Glacier Alley, the appeal lies in the succession of views: ice tongues appear one after another as the ship follows the mountains. Separate landings along the alley should not be assumed merely from the route name.

Other natural stops on this cruise include [Ainsworth Bay](/chile/place/ainsworth-bay/), with its subantarctic forest and Marinelli moraine, and [Tucker Islets](/chile/place/tucker-islets/), known for seabird watching. They reveal different aspects of [Chile's natural environment](/chile/).

## How to plan a visit and prepare

For Pia, sea conditions are more important than catching a particular shade of blue ice in a photograph. Weather changes quickly around the Beagle Channel. Clouds may obscure mountain tops, wind affects the stability of small boats, and rain and wet rocks complicate walking.

Bring layered clothing, a waterproof jacket, sturdy footwear for natural trails and water protection for your equipment. Even during warmer Southern Hemisphere months, wind and cold feel sharper on a small boat than inside the ship.

When choosing a cruise, ask **how much time is allocated to Pia itself, whether a landing is permitted and what walking options are offered**. A photo of Pia in a catalog does not prove that every Beagle Channel itinerary includes a landing at this glacier. Our [Fjords of Tierra del Fuego tour](/multi-country/tour/tierra-del-fuego-fjords/) explicitly includes the stop.

The closest travel category is [cruises and expeditions](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/). For anyone interested in geological processes, Pia demonstrates how glaciers have shaped the landforms of South America's island-studded south.

## Frequently asked questions about Pia Glacier

### Where is Pia Glacier?

In Chilean Tierra del Fuego, beside Pia Fjord in the northwestern part of the Beagle Channel area. The stated itinerary reaches it by sea.

### Can I walk up to the glacier?

A walk to a lookout is offered, and depending on the itinerary and conditions, a more demanding hike along the moraine may be possible. **The tourist program does not offer walking on the glacier itself.**

### Should I choose Pia or Glacier Alley?

They are different experiences that follow one another on the [Fjords of Tierra del Fuego cruise](/multi-country/tour/tierra-del-fuego-fjords/): Pia may provide a shore viewpoint, while Glacier Alley offers panoramas from the ship.

### Could the landing at Pia be canceled?

Yes. Wind, waves and safe landing conditions determine the crew's decisions. A scheduled itinerary stop is not an unconditional guarantee of going ashore in every kind of weather.

## Tours via Pia Glacier: which cruise should you choose?

[Pia Glacier](/chile/place/pia-glacier/) lies in a remote area of Chilean Tierra del Fuego, descending to the water of the fjord of the same name. Travelers reach it on an expedition ship: a typical visit includes views from the deck, a trip in small Zodiac boats and a walk to a lookout. Marine weather and landing conditions are important considerations.

Here you will find {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with the glacier included on the main route. One is a standalone fjords cruise, while the other combines the southern maritime region with high-altitude Bolivia, the Atacama Desert, Patagonia and Argentina.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_fordy_ognennoj_zemli,tour_source_kruiznyj_tur_po_luchshim_mestam_argentiny_chili_i_bolivii}}

## Five days in the fjords or an 18-day journey

[Fjords of Tierra del Fuego](/multi-country/tour/tierra-del-fuego-fjords/) is a separate **5-day** sea voyage from [Punta Arenas](/chile/place/punta-arenas/) to [Ushuaia](/argentina/place/ushuaia/). On day three, the ship approaches Pia Glacier and then sails through [Glacier Alley](/chile/place/glacier-alley/). Earlier stops include [Ainsworth Bay](/chile/place/ainsworth-bay/) and [Tucker Islets](/chile/place/tucker-islets/). Wulaia Bay and the Cape Horn area follow, although individual landings depend on the weather.

[Argentina, Chile, Bolivia and Patagonia in 18 Days](/multi-country/tour/argentina-chile-bolivia-cruise-tour-18-days/) is a longer journey through three countries. It starts in Santiago and Atacama, continues to Bolivia's high-altitude lagoons and Uyuni Salt Flat, then Torres del Paine. The sea voyage through southern Chilean channels begins after that. Pia Glacier appears on day nine of the trip. The cruise ends in Ushuaia, followed by Buenos Aires and Bariloche.

| Your priority | Suitable format |
|---|---|
| Time at sea | 5 days among the fjords |
| Three countries | 18-day journey |
| Fewer flights | Standalone cruise |
| Varied natural zones | Longer itinerary |

Both include a maritime section at Pia. But a shared glacier stop does not make the overall trips equivalent: most of the shorter cruise is spent aboard, while the 18-day journey involves flights, lengthy drives and high-altitude locations.

## How the glacier landing works

On Fjords of Tierra del Fuego, the ship enters Pia Fjord from the Beagle Channel. Guests travel ashore in Zodiac boats and choose between two walking options: a gentler route to a viewpoint or a more demanding climb along the glacier's lateral moraine. Views take in the ice, mountain slopes and fjord water.

On the longer journey, Pia is also a stop on the sea passage. Afterwards, the ship continues toward [Glacier Alley](/chile/place/glacier-alley/), where other glaciers descending from the Darwin Mountains can be seen from the water. These are separate geographic features. Watching glaciers from a ship is not equivalent to landing at each one.

Physical demands depend on the shore route chosen. The moraine may have stones, wet ground and uneven terrain. If you only want to view the glacier without a lengthy ascent, discuss the shorter option and any personal limitations in advance. The expedition team determines the final landing arrangements based on conditions that day.

## Weather, season and safety

Even in the sailing season, southern Tierra del Fuego remains windy and cool. Weather changes faster than in many popular coastal destinations. In strong winds or unsafe conditions, small-boat departures and shore excursions may be changed or canceled. **Pia's inclusion in the itinerary does not guarantee a landing in all weather.**

Bring a waterproof jacket, a warm layer, shoes with good grip and splash protection for equipment, both for the deck and shore. Warm clothing is useful even with a relatively calm forecast, as wind makes exposed water feel colder.

Before choosing a departure, compare specific dates, embarkation and disembarkation ports, nights aboard and itinerary-change conditions. If seeing the glacier up close is your priority, clarify what happens when landing is impossible. A planned shore walk and a confirmed landing are not the same thing.

## What to combine with Pia Glacier

The shorter marine route offers a succession of visits to remote southern bays. Expect coastal birdwatching, subantarctic forest shores and sea views of mountains. A day at [Wulaia Bay](/chile/place/wulaia-bay/) differs from the glacier section, featuring the archipelago's history and cultural geography.

If you also want to experience Patagonia on land, compare [Chile tours](/chile/tour/) visiting Torres del Paine. They reveal mountain lakes, valleys and glaciers in a different way. An expedition cruise reaches fjord regions that ordinary sightseeing vehicles cannot access.

Travelers interested in [cruises and expeditions](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/) should compare actual sailing days and planned landings. Choose the longer journey through three countries if Atacama, Uyuni and Argentina appeal equally and you are comfortable with the additional logistical demands.

## Frequently asked questions about Pia Glacier tours

### Can I drive to Pia Glacier?

Ada Tours' standard itineraries reach the glacier by expedition ship. There is no sightseeing road access to the stated location on these tours.

### On which day of the cruise do you visit?

On the [five-day Fjords of Tierra del Fuego voyage](/multi-country/tour/tierra-del-fuego-fjords/), Pia is scheduled for day three. On the [18-day journey](/multi-country/tour/argentina-chile-bolivia-cruise-tour-18-days/), it appears on day nine of the complete trip. Actual landing arrangements depend on weather.

### Are Pia Glacier and Glacier Alley the same place?

No. [Pia](/chile/place/pia-glacier/) is one glacier beside a fjord, while [Glacier Alley](/chile/place/glacier-alley/) is a marine passage with views of multiple glaciers. On the itineraries described, they follow one another.

### How should I choose between 5 and 18 days?

Choose the five-day trip for a concentrated cruise through the fjords between Chile and Argentina. The 18-day route combines that voyage with Bolivia's highlands, Atacama, land-based Patagonia and Argentine cities.

## Plaza Sotomayor: the historic heart of port-side Valparaíso

**Plaza Sotomayor is one of the best places to begin discovering Valparaíso's maritime history.** It occupies the flat waterfront part of the city, between old urban buildings and the harbor. Architecture, monuments and maritime life come together in one space.

The square's main landmark is the Monument to the Heroes of Iquique, commemorating the naval battle of 1879. On one edge stands the historic former Intendancy building, now occupied by the command of Chile's First Naval Zone. In the other direction, the route leads to Muelle Prat pier, with harbor views and boats offering sightseeing trips around the bay.

On our [Hidden Treasures of Bolivia and Chile itinerary](/multi-country/tour/bolivia-chile-hidden-treasures-16-days/), the square is included in a city day covering Valparaíso and Viña del Mar. It is a convenient starting point for exploring the old port before moving toward the stairways and houses on the hills.

## What are the main sights on the square?

### Monument to the Heroes of Iquique

The memorial honors Chilean sailors who fought at Iquique in the War of the Pacific in 1879. It occupies a prominent place on the square and helps explain why important maritime commemorations take place here.

The monument is a historical symbol of a port nation. Viewing it only as an attractive stone structure misses Valparaíso's connections with the navy, commerce and 19th-century military history. The Battle of Iquique occupies an important place in Chilean historical memory; a guided excursion is a useful setting for discussing the details and interpretations.

### Facades around the square

The square is surrounded by administrative, commercial and port-related buildings from different periods. One notable landmark is the [former Intendancy, now the First Naval Zone headquarters](/chile/place/navy-headquarters-valparaiso/). Its symmetrical facade, ornamentation and large central section distinguish it from ordinary port buildings.

Other historic buildings show how the port city grew. Rather than trying to visit every facade separately, stand in the middle of the square and look around: the ensemble took shape over several periods of Valparaíso's development.

In 1979, the square and its surroundings received protected *Zona Típica* status in Chile, recognizing an area of historical urban significance. This designation values the ensemble as a whole, not just one monument. It does not mean the interiors of all buildings are open to tourists.

## How the square connects to Valparaíso's port and hills

From Sotomayor it is easy to walk toward Prat pier. The scene changes from architectural facades to harbor waters, vessels and port activity. The pier is best treated as a separate stage of a city walk, rather than literally part of the square.

In the other direction, streets lead toward the city's historic hills. [Cerro Concepción](/chile/place/cerro-concepcion/), [Paseo Gervasoni](/chile/place/paseo-gervasoni/) and [Paseo Atkinson](/chile/place/paseo-atkinson/) show a different Valparaíso: steep streets, colorful facades, promenades and views over rooftops. If time allows, combining the square with one hill gives a fuller impression of the city than visiting either alone.

To compare historic Valparaíso with its neighboring seaside resort, explore [Valparaíso and Viña del Mar](/chile/place/valparaiso-vina-del-mar/). You do not need to spend a whole day on the square itself; it functions as the starting point of a longer tour.

## Planning a walk without unnecessary transfers

For a first visit, a sensible sequence is to see the monument and historic facades, walk toward the harbor, then choose a route up one of the hills. The square itself is easily explored on foot, but Valparaíso's slopes and staircases begin farther on. Travelers who find climbs difficult should arrange transport between the flat waterfront and the hilly part of the city in advance.

The open paved square can be bright and hot in sunshine, while cool winds blow in from the ocean. Comfortable footwear and sun protection help when walking both the square and neighboring streets. City festivals, commemorations and other events can affect normal movement across the square, so check access to individual areas for your travel dates.

If culture and history are your interests, you can also explore [Chile's cultural and historical itineraries](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/chile/). The exact stops depend on the trip you choose, not simply on the places listed in a general city guide.

## Frequently asked questions about Plaza Sotomayor

### What are the main sights on the square?

The Monument to the Heroes of Iquique and the surrounding historic buildings, especially the [former Intendancy](/chile/place/navy-headquarters-valparaiso/). Afterwards, walk toward Prat pier.

### Is there an entrance fee to walk around the square?

The square is an open public space, and no ticket is needed for a normal walk. Individual buildings and organized events may have their own access rules.

### Is the square on one of Valparaíso's hills?

No. It lies in the flat waterfront part of the city. For elevated views, continue toward a hill such as [Cerro Concepción](/chile/place/cerro-concepcion/).

### Can I combine the square with Viña del Mar?

Yes. Both feature in some sightseeing programs, including our [16-day Ada Tours Bolivia and Chile itinerary](/multi-country/tour/bolivia-chile-hidden-treasures-16-days/). For a particular trip, account for driving times and the number of planned stops.
